tax.title: Colorado wildfire tax credit
tax.lead: The state gives back what a homeowner pays a contractor for wildfire mitigation on their own land, as a credit on their Colorado income tax.

p: Tax years 2025 and 2026: 100% of the cost, up to $1,000.
From tax year 2027: up to $2,000, and any credit above what they owe is paid out as a refund.
Before 2027, credit above what they owe in state tax is lost. It is not refunded and does not carry forward.
An owner of record of private land in Colorado. A recorded lease also counts. Only one person per ownership group can claim.
Income limit: federal taxable income up to $129,200 for 2025. The 2026 limit is not published yet. From 2027: income (AGI) up to $300,000.
There is no wildfire-zone test. Any private land in Colorado can qualify.
Owned by an LLC or other company: send them to an accountant. The rules for companies are unsettled.
Defensible space around buildings, fuel breaks, thinning to protect buildings, and dealing with what we cut: chipping, piling, lop-and-scatter, hauling off or burning.
It has to meet Colorado State Forest Service or Division of Fire Prevention and Control standards.
Only what they pay a contractor counts. Their own equipment or labor does not.
Anything paid by a grant or cost-share. On a Douglas County cost-share job, only the homeowner's own half can go toward the credit.
Inspection or certification fees. Buying or renting equipment.
They claim it themselves, on form DR 0104CR filed with their Colorado return, with our receipts attached.
We give them an itemized invoice that separates the qualifying work, and a note of the standard we worked to.

say: Colorado has a tax credit for this: 100% of what you pay us, up to $1,000 this year, and $2,000 from 2027.
We itemize the invoice so the qualifying work is easy to claim.
Your accountant can confirm how it works for you.
dont: "We handle the paperwork for you." We don't prepare or file tax returns.
"You'll get $1,000 back." It depends on their income and their tax bill.
Any example that stacks a grant and the credit on the same dollars.
sources: Colorado Department of Revenue, Income Tax Topics: Wildfire Mitigation Measures (read in full 21 Aug 2026; 2026 limit re-checked as TBD 2 Oct 2026)
C.R.S. 39-22-543 as amended by HB26-1289 (enacted text)

insurance.title: Insurance and mitigation
insurance.lead: Since 1 July 2026, Colorado law (HB25-1182) requires insurers that use wildfire risk scores to tell homeowners their score and how mitigation is counted, to give credit for documented mitigation, and to let homeowners appeal.

p: Ask their insurer for their wildfire risk score and the discounts it gives for mitigation.
An insurer that gives mitigation discounts has to post them, with the amounts, on its website. One that gives none has to say so.
After the work, they send the insurer the evidence and ask for their score to be reviewed. The insurer has 30 days to update it or explain in writing why not. They can appeal.
Receipts and photos of the work.
Letters or reports from the mitigation contractor, which is us.
Inspection reports from a fire department or county, and community certificates such as Firewise.
On every fire job we give dated before-and-after photos and an itemized record they can send.

blocks.h: What nobody can tell them in advance
p: How big the discount will be. The law sets no percentage, and every insurer is different.
Some insurers build mitigation into the score instead of giving a separate discount.
These rules cover admitted insurers and the Colorado FAIR Plan, not non-admitted (surplus lines) insurers.

say: Colorado now makes your insurer tell you your wildfire score and what they give for mitigation.
We'll give you before-and-after photos and a written record of the work to send them.
dont: "This will lower your premium," or any percentage.
sources: Division of Insurance Regulation 5-1-28 (3 CCR 702-5): draft text read 2 Oct 2026. The adopted version may differ in detail; its effective date is reported inconsistently, so none is given here.

grants.lead: Grant money for homeowners depends on the county. This sheet changes with the town you're in.

douglas.title: Douglas County cost-share

p: Douglas County pays 50% of a homeowner's wildfire mitigation project, up to $25,000. Community projects can get up to $50,000, and community chipping up to $7,500.
The county pays its half straight to the contractor after inspecting the finished work.
The 2026 round is closed. The next round has not been announced.
The homeowner applies with two contractor bids, a scope of work and a site map. The county visits with the homeowner and the contractor before approving.
Work starts only after the award is signed. They then have 10 months to finish. Work done before the award is not covered.
Homeowners can use any qualified contractor. The county keeps a preferred list and encourages people to use it. Sixfold is not on that list.

say: Douglas County runs a 50% cost-share for this. This year's round has closed. We can quote now so you're ready for the next one.
Our bid can be one of the two the county asks for.
dont: "We're on the county's approved list." We're not.
"You'll get the grant." Awards are competitive.
"Start now and the county will pay half." Work before the award isn't covered.
sources: Douglas County, Wildfire Mitigation Cost-Share Program page (read 2 Oct 2026)
Douglas County, cost-share contractor list, August 2026: "Residents may choose any qualified contractor to complete eligible work."

p: We have not found a cost-share for homeowners here.
Teller County and Woodland Park have a $1 million state grant for a fuel buffer around Woodland Park. It protects utilities and roads. It is not money for homeowners.
The state tax credit and insurance. Both apply here.

wells.title: Wells

blocks.h: A well is not a loophole
p: Most private wells on lots under 35 acres, permitted since 8 May 1972, are for household use only: water inside the house.
They may not legally water a lawn or garden at all. Not two days a week, not at night, not ever. It is a condition of the well permit and has nothing to do with the drought.
These may carry fuller well rights, which can include up to one acre of lawn and garden.
"I'm on a well, so the restrictions don't apply" is often exactly backwards.
Ask what the well permit allows before quoting an overseed. If it is household use only, the seed has no legal water: sell aeration, mowing or cleanup instead.
The permit is the owner's responsibility, not ours. But seed nobody can water is a job that fails.

sources: Colorado Division of Water Resources, Guideline 2023-1

p: Only for homes on Colorado Springs Utilities water.
Lets them water more often than three days a week, and in the daytime hours that are normally banned: 42 days for seed, 28 for sod. Only needed for sprinklers.
For non-native seed they need a lab soil test, or receipts for 4 cubic yards of soil amendment per 1,000 sq ft. For a qualifying native mix, just the seed receipt.
The permit belongs to the water customer, not to us. We can walk them through applying: online, or at 2855 Mesa Rd.
No fee appears in the utility's own permit document. Don't quote one.

say.title: What to say

p: Water the lawn thoroughly the day before, so the machine pulls deep plugs. On hard, dry ground the plugs come out short, or the machine bounces.
Water soon after, and keep watering regularly: the holes need water to heal over.
Colorado State University Extension: don't core-aerate a lawn that is totally brown or dormant from water restrictions.
Denver Water banned all lawn watering from 1 October. It doesn't reach any town we work.

say: Aeration still works on the allowed days: water the lawn the day before and soon after.
Which water provider are you on?
If you're on Colorado Springs Utilities, there's a permit that lets you water more often while new seed comes in. I can show you how to get it.
Water the lawn a day or two before we come out.
dont: Anything that sounds like a promise the seed will come up. We don't water and we don't guarantee germination.
A watering schedule for a provider, unless you checked its page this week.
Aerating a lawn that's brown or dormant.
"You're on a well, so the restrictions don't apply." Often the opposite.
